值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析中共中央軍委高層遭遇大規模清洗的政治震盪，及其對台海軍事局勢的潛在衝擊。
  • 詳解張又俠、劉振立等具備實戰與指揮背景的核心將領落馬後，對解放軍聯合作戰協同能力的實質癱瘓。
  • 從人性自保與官僚體系視角，揭示整肅氛圍如何導致前線指揮官陷入「不求有功、但求無過」的決策困境。

摘要

軍委高層劇震與大清洗現象

作者阿牛指出，中共中央軍委近期迎來前所未見的政治風暴，包括被視為習近平軍中核心盟友、少數具備實戰經驗的軍委副主席張又俠，以及負責擬定作戰計畫的聯合參謀部參謀長劉振立等人均傳遭到整肅。根據智庫 CSIS 的數據，近年已有數十名中將、上將及百名高階將領遭到調查或去職，波及陸軍、海軍、空軍、火箭軍與後勤裝備等多個部門，導致軍委內部嚴重缺乏熟悉大型聯合作戰的專業將領，多數留任者僅具備政工或紀檢背景。

作戰協同重挫與指揮體系癱瘓

作者分析，大規模進攻台灣是現代軍事史上極度複雜的兩棲登陸作戰，高度仰賴海空封鎖、雷達摧毀、火箭打擊、後勤補給及電子網絡戰的精密協同。如今主導聯合作戰核心部門的將領接連落馬，直接衝擊部隊備戰狀態。更嚴重的是，頻繁的清洗在軍隊內部引發極大的人性恐慌，將領們每天上班的首要考量變成「如何避免成為下一個落馬者」，導致基層與中階指揮官不敢依戰況臨機處置，全面陷入「層層推諉、等待指令」的被動局面，對戰場應變構成致命隱患。

反腐名義下的清洗與對台攻防抉擇

對於高層將領連番遭撤換的原因，中共官方始終定調為軍隊反腐，作者認為解放軍內部買官賣官與工程腐敗確實嚴重，但此舉亦加劇了權力核心的政治猜忌。軍委高層幾乎被淘空現況，帶來了兩種截然不同的推論：其一，缺乏具作戰經驗的指揮官與成熟的作戰體系，可能使習近平在短期內更難輕舉妄動；其二，一旦軍隊完全換上唯命是從的親信，決策缺乏專業反對意見，未來反而可能在誤判下做出更激進的軍事冒險。

================================================

If you were a general in the Communist army today, and your predecessor was arrested, the person before that was arrested, your superior was arrested, your superior’s superior was arrested, and even Zhang Youxia, who everyone thought had a great relationship with Xi Jinping, was arrested—what would your primary goal be when you go to work? Would it really be to study how to win a war in the Taiwan Strait? Or would it be how to act today so that I don’t become the next Youxia? This is a very realistic question of human nature. More seriously, if Xi Jinping frames the unification of Taiwan as his. historical mission, but ends up losing, it wouldn't just be the failure of the Communist army; it would be Xi Jinping’s personal failure and could even turn into a political crisis for the CCP regime. People often ask about the map in the background. This map isn't just A-Niu’s dream of the Republic of China’s territory; it is how the Republic of China should look in the hearts of 1.4 billion sons and daughters of China! We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of restoring the Republic and rebuilding the republic. We have launched a merchandise bundle featuring a map poster, hanging scroll,. pillow, and a Republic of China flag keychain. Kids make choices, but I want them all; take them all home for just 1911. Plus, on both platforms, you get free shipping on orders over 699. Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so hurry up and grab yours! Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Recently, something outrageous happened with the Communist army across the strait. On August 28, 2026, only two of the seven giants in the CCP’s Central Military Commission remained, with even Xi Jinping’s closest allies, Zhang Youxia and Liu, being removed. You must realize. , these two are not just ordinary figures. Zhang Youxia is the first-ranked Vice Chairman of the Military Commission, second only to Xi Jinping, and could be called the only person in the entire Communist army with real power and actual combat experience. Liu Zhenli is the Chief of the Joint Staff; he is the mastermind and chief planner of the Communist army’s invasion plans. And the result? One is Xi Jinping’s biggest military pillar, and the other is the key figure responsible for waging war—both have. been completely purged. I must briefly explain here that the CCP has both a "Party Central Military Commission" and a "State Central Military Commission," two structures that are nominally parallel but highly overlapping in reality. On August 28, the officials specifically handled the State Central Military Commission positions. While the Party’s military positions still require separate public procedures , in terms of actual political reality, the original top military leadership team has indeed been shattered.

So today, let's discuss an interesting question: now that the Central Military Commission has been nearly emptied out, does Xi Jinping still dare to attack Taiwan? Many people, seeing the recent massive purge in the PLA, might first think: "That’s great, the generals are all being arrested, so what does the PLA have left to attack Taiwan with?" But is it really that simple? I personally feel there might be two completely opposite ways to interpret this. One is that Xi might now be even less likely to attack, but the other is even. more terrifying: once Xi has finished purging the military, he might actually be even more willing to strike. Which one is it? Actually, Xi Jinping's purging of the PLA didn't just start today. Soon after taking power in 2012, he began restructuring the military. You might be familiar with former CMC Vice Chairmen Xu Caihou and Guo Boxiong, or later, Fang Fenghui and Zhang Yang, though maybe you don't recognize them. Back then, many felt Xi was primarily clearing out military factions left over. from the Jiang Zemin era, while also tackling the severe issues of selling official positions and corruption within the PLA. That round of purges was already quite large in scale, but compared to the one launched in 2023, that earlier effort might just be considered an appetizer. Starting in 2023, first the Rocket Force had issues, then Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared and was dismissed; former Defense Minister Wei Fenghe was also handled. Next came Miao Hua, Director of the CMC Political Work. Department, and CMC Vice Chairman He Weidong. Then, by 2026, even Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were in trouble. The most shocking case here is Zhang Youxia, because he wasn't just any subordinate of Xi Jinping. He has long been viewed by the outside world as one of Xi's most important and loyal allies in the military, and he is also one of the few high-ranking PLA generals with actual combat experience— yet even Zhang Youxia is being investigated. So, this can no longer be simply explained as Xi removing old remnants to. replace them with his own people, because even those originally considered "his own" can now be arrested just the same. CSIS compiled a very worthy set of data in February 2026. They calculated that since 2022, at least 36 PLA generals and lieutenant generals have been formally purged or disciplined, while another 65 high-ranking officers have not appeared in public for a long time, presumably investigated or removed. In other words, if you count those who.

have disappeared, over 100 high-ranking PLA officers have been affected. Moreover, those taken down aren't concentrated in any single branch; they span the Army, Navy, Air Force, Rocket Force, Armed Police, and Theater Commands, as well as CMC departments responsible for joint operations, political work, and logistics and equipment. In fact, CSIS pointed out a very serious issue as early as February 2026: there were no longer any top-level leaders in the Central Military Commission with a background in operational systems; those. who remained were primarily from political work or disciplinary inspection backgrounds, rather than professional generals capable of managing large-scale joint operations. What we are seeing today is not just a few corrupt generals being arrested, but a drastic restructuring taking place within the entire PLA high command. Even by August 25th, the PLA publicly solicited leads on procurement violations within the Rocket Force, indicating that this round of purging is far from over. So the question is, if Xi Jinping is truly preparing to attack Taiwan...Why would he choose this exact moment to replace his highest-ranking generals one by one? If we look at this from a purely military perspective, I believe the answer is quite easy to understand. This , of course, affects the PLA's combat readiness, because attacking Taiwan is not like fighting a typical border war. Don't think for a moment that Xi can just sit in Beijing, say "Comrades, liberate Taiwan tomorrow at 8:00 AM," and hundreds of ships will just sail. over on their own. Launching a large-scale military operation against Taiwan—especially with the goal of an amphibious invasion and occupation— would likely be one of the most complex joint operations in modern military history. The PLA would first need to strike radar, airfields, and air defense systems; the Air Force must secure air superiority; the Navy must control the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters; the Army must prepare for amphibious landings; logistics must ferry troops, shells, fuel, and gear across the Strait ; all while managing electronic warfare. , cyber warfare, satellite intel, and drones—all must be synchronized, and if one link fails, the outcome could be entirely different. But now, the very people responsible for these tasks are getting into trouble one after another, the most typical example being Liu Zhenli. He was originally a chief of the Joint Staff Department. What is the Joint Staff Department? Simply put, it is the core unit within the PLA that is closest to knowing how a war would actually be fought. If you replace a business manager today , it might not necessarily affect the whole company.

But if you were preparing to launch the biggest project in history tomorrow, and the project director, technical lead, operations lead, and logistics lead were all under investigation, would you dare take on the job? A normal person would certainly hesitate . And even more seriously, this purge of generals doesn't just leave positions empty—it risks paralyzing the entire organization, making everyone afraid to make a decision. If you were a PLA general today, your predecessor was arrested, your predecessor’s predecessor was arrested,. your superior was arrested, your superior’s superior was arrested, and even Zhang Youxia, who everyone thought was close to Xi Jinping, was arrested— what would be your first goal when you go to work? Would it really be to study how to win a war in the Taiwan Strait? Or would it be to figure out how to avoid becoming the next Youxia? This is a very realistic question of human nature, and it is actually extremely dangerous for the military. Because one of the things most needed on the battlefield is for mid-to-lower-level commanders to make. judgments on their own under incomplete information. But in a highly politicized military where everyone looks out for themselves, the most common outcomes are "I don't want to make a mistake" and "I don't want to be held responsible"— people just follow orders and push everything up the chain of command. For a peacetime bureaucracy, this might just mean poor efficiency, but on the battlefield, it could be a matter of life and death. This brings up a second question: Why is Xi Jinping arresting so many people? Official CCP rhetoric always claims it's. anti-corruption, and this reason cannot be completely dismissed, because corruption in the PLA has historically been severe. You have to pay to get promoted, there's graft in construction, and arms procurement generates huge profits. So, Xi might truly believe that a corrupt military cannot win a war. From this perspective, his purge of the military has some military justification . But on the other hand, a purge on this scale creates another problem: If the Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission, the Defense Minister, the. Rocket Force commander, the Director of the Political Work Department, and the Chief of the Joint Staff all have issues one after another, doesn't that prove that Xi Jinping doesn't even trust his own military? If he truly believed the PLA was ready, why would he keep arresting people? Furthermore, the cost of a Taiwan Strait war is simply too high. If they lose, it wouldn't just be tens of thousands of troops lost; it would likely be the decades of military prestige the CCP has built up. They could face military intervention from the US, Japan, and.

other nations, and suffer international economic sanctions. China's exports, finance, technology, and energy supplies could all be severely impacted. More seriously, if Xi Jinping has framed the unification of Taiwan as his historical mission, but he ends up losing, it wouldn't just be a defeat for the PLA. It would be a personal failure, and could potentially turn into a political crisis for the CCP regime itself. So, following this logic, I believe these recent large-scale purges will indeed reduce the confidence to launch an. all-out war in the Taiwan Strait in the short term. This is not to say that the PLA lacks the capability to conduct blockades, military exercises, missile threats, or even localized military operations. In fact, even with the continuous purges of high-level officials, the PLA’s gray-zone pressure around Taiwan has never ceased. CSIS data also indicates that the CCP’s military and coast guard activities around Taiwan continue to increase this year, so we cannot simply say, "The PLA generals have all been arrested, so we. are now safe." That would be too optimistic. A more accurate statement would be that these purges increase the uncertainty of launching a large-scale joint operation , but they do not mean the CCP has lost the ability to use force. The expert survey conducted by CSIS this year is also quite interesting; only about 13%of the surveyed experts believe these purges are severe enough to prevent the CCP from using large-scale military force over the next two years, while about 57%believe the purges have. caused significant problems for military readiness, but not to the extent of rendering them unable to act. So, we cannot rejoice too soon, because the story does not end here. Now, let’s look at it from another angle : assume Xi Jinping purged the military not just because of corruption, but because he wanted to build an army that absolutely obeys the CCP Central Committee, and ultimately, absolutely obeys Xi Jinping’s orders. What would be the result? In the short term, it would certainly be chaotic because a large. number of high-level officials were replaced, but what if all the new generals are in place after a few years ? And all these new generals know that Zhang Youxia was purged, He Weidong was purged, Miao Hua was purged, Li Shangfu was purged, and Liu Zhenli was also purged. If even these top military officials, once considered Xi Jinping’s closest associates, could face trouble, what will those left behind learn? The answer is likely four words: absolute obedience. That is where the problem arises. If one day Xi Jinping truly decides to take action against.

Taiwan, no one would dare tell him, " Chairman, you can't; we aren't ready yet , the success rate of a landing isn't as high as you imagine, the U.S. might intervene, Japan might intervene, and we cannot bear the cost of economic sanctions." That is my real concern, because whether a nation’s military is dangerous depends not only on how many planes, warships, or fighters it has, but also on whether its top leader receives accurate information. People often ask if Xi Jinping will go crazy and attack Taiwan; I don't really. like that framing, because the person who starts a war doesn't necessarily think they are crazy. When many catastrophic wars are launched , the decision-makers may believe their judgment is perfectly rational; the real problem is what kind of information they are receiving. If everyone below knows exactly what the Chairman wants to hear, reports may gradually shift to saying the ROC military is demoralized, the U.S. won't dare intervene, our missiles can paralyze Taiwan, the conflict will end in days, and the Taiwanese people will welcome us. When one person says it,. then two, then ten, the world the supreme leader eventually sees may be completely different from reality; this is the classic risk of a highly centralized, autocratic system. Democratic systems are noisy— parliaments bicker, the media criticizes , and opposition parties attack—which allows for the open expression of dissenting views. It may look inefficient, but this noise serves a vital function: it can identify a mistake before the nation commits a grave one. However, a highly authoritarian system is the opposite. Decisions appear swift, with the. leader's word instantly executed by everyone below. The question is, what happens if the supreme leader is wrong? Who hits the brakes? Therefore, when observing the ongoing purges in the PLA, we shouldn't just ask how many generals are left; the real question is whether the remaining generals dare to tell Xi Jinping the truth. If the purge results in a more professional, better-connected, and more efficient military, it would certainly boost combat capabilities. But if it builds a military that values only loyalty over expertise—where they only report good news and never bad, claiming they will fulfill the Chairman’s tasks without anyone daring to say this war cannot be fought—that could actually be more dangerous for the Republic of China. Ultimately, with the Central Military Commission nearly hollowed out, does Xi Jinping still dare to attack Taiwan? My answer is that in the short term, it may be harder for him to fight, but that doesn't mean he is necessarily less likely to fight in the long term. The investigation of so many top-level officials will inevitably disrupt.

command, personnel, operational planning , and organizational trust. For a target like Taiwan, which requires extremely complex joint combat capabilities, long-term instability in the high command is certainly not a good thing. So, if someone claims Xi is preparing for an imminent full-scale invasion by dismantling his entire top military command team, I find that argument inherently contradictory. Conversely, we cannot assume the risk of a Taiwan Strait war has disappeared just because the Central Military Commission. is left with only two main members; Xi Jinping's goal may be to purge those he deems unreliable and rebuild a military command system he can control completely . If I were to condense today's conclusion into one sentence, it would be this: it might be harder for Xi Jinping to fight now, but that doesn't mean he wants to fight any less. What's even more concerning is that the biggest problem for the PLA today may not be a shortage of generals, but whether any of the remaining ones still dare to say no. A CCP that possesses. numerous missiles, nuclear weapons, aircraft carriers, and a complete industrial system is certainly cause for vigilance. However, a CCP that holds these weapons while centralizing all decision-making increasingly into the hands of one man, Xi Jinping, is perhaps even more alarming. This is because decisions of war and peace are no longer determined by collective discussion or the judgment of professional military commanders, but by what one man, Xi Jinping, truly believes. Therefore, the clearing out of the Central Military Commission—while some. might jokingly say it’s like gaining over 100 generals without firing a shot as in the days before the Civil War, or praising Comrade Xi for his "hard work" —is not entirely good news for the Republic of China. What we truly need to observe is whom Xi Jinping will appoint to fill these vacancies in the Central Military Commission next. Who will take control of the new Joint Staff Department, and will the high-level positions in the various military branches and theater commands be fully replenished? Will these people rise to power because of their professional competence, or because of their political loyalty? If the upper echelons of the PLA are gradually filled with those who are highly trusted by Xi Jinping, the question we will really need to ask is not whether the PLA can still fight, but when Xi Jinping truly gives the order to attack, who will be left to stop him? This may be the truly significant impact of this latest purge within the Central Military Commission on the situation in the Taiwan Strait. Having said this, I want to return to the purpose of this channel. What I have always wanted to discuss with everyone is that we care about the Taiwan Strait, the PLA, and.

  • 從人性自保與官僚體系視角，揭示整肅氛圍如何導致前線指揮官陷入「不求有功、但求無過」的決策困境。

摘要

軍委高層劇震與大清洗現象

作者阿牛指出，中共中央軍委近期迎來前所未見的政治風暴，包括被視為習近平軍中核心盟友、少數具備實戰經驗的軍委副主席張又俠，以及負責擬定作戰計畫的聯合參謀部參謀長劉振立等人均傳遭到整肅。根據智庫 CSIS 的數據，近年已有數十名中將、上將及百名高階將領遭到調查或去職，波及陸軍、海軍、空軍、火箭軍與後勤裝備等多個部門，導致軍委內部嚴重缺乏熟悉大型聯合作戰的專業將領，多數留任者僅具備政工或紀檢背景。

作戰協同重挫與指揮體系癱瘓

作者分析，大規模進攻台灣是現代軍事史上極度複雜的兩棲登陸作戰，高度仰賴海空封鎖、雷達摧毀、火箭打擊、後勤補給及電子網絡戰的精密協同。如今主導聯合作戰核心部門的將領接連落馬，直接衝擊部隊備戰狀態。更嚴重的是，頻繁的清洗在軍隊內部引發極大的人性恐慌，將領們每天上班的首要考量變成「如何避免成為下一個落馬者」，導致基層與中階指揮官不敢依戰況臨機處置，全面陷入「層層推諉、等待指令」的被動局面，對戰場應變構成致命隱患。

反腐名義下的清洗與對台攻防抉擇

對於高層將領連番遭撤換的原因，中共官方始終定調為軍隊反腐，作者認為解放軍內部買官賣官與工程腐敗確實嚴重，但此舉亦加劇了權力核心的政治猜忌。軍委高層幾乎被淘空現況，帶來了兩種截然不同的推論：其一，缺乏具作戰經驗的指揮官與成熟的作戰體系，可能使習近平在短期內更難輕舉妄動；其二，一旦軍隊完全換上唯命是從的親信，決策缺乏專業反對意見，未來反而可能在誤判下做出更激進的軍事冒險。

================================================

If you were a general in the Communist army today, and your predecessor was arrested, the person before that was arrested, your superior was arrested, your superior’s superior was arrested, and even Zhang Youxia, who everyone thought had a great relationship with Xi Jinping, was arrested—what would your primary goal be when you go to work? Would it really be to study how to win a war in the Taiwan Strait? Or would it be how to act today so that I don’t become the next Youxia? This is a very realistic question of human nature. More seriously, if Xi Jinping frames the unification of Taiwan as his. historical mission, but ends up losing, it wouldn't just be the failure of the Communist army; it would be Xi Jinping’s personal failure and could even turn into a political crisis for the CCP regime. People often ask about the map in the background. This map isn't just A-Niu’s dream of the Republic of China’s territory; it is how the Republic of China should look in the hearts of 1.4 billion sons and daughters of China! We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of restoring the Republic and rebuilding the republic. We have launched a merchandise bundle featuring a map poster, hanging scroll,. pillow, and a Republic of China flag keychain. Kids make choices, but I want them all; take them all home for just 1911. Plus, on both platforms, you get free shipping on orders over 699. Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so hurry up and grab yours! Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Recently, something outrageous happened with the Communist army across the strait. On August 28, 2026, only two of the seven giants in the CCP’s Central Military Commission remained, with even Xi Jinping’s closest allies, Zhang Youxia and Liu, being removed. You must realize. , these two are not just ordinary figures. Zhang Youxia is the first-ranked Vice Chairman of the Military Commission, second only to Xi Jinping, and could be called the only person in the entire Communist army with real power and actual combat experience. Liu Zhenli is the Chief of the Joint Staff; he is the mastermind and chief planner of the Communist army’s invasion plans. And the result? One is Xi Jinping’s biggest military pillar, and the other is the key figure responsible for waging war—both have. been completely purged. I must briefly explain here that the CCP has both a "Party Central Military Commission" and a "State Central Military Commission," two structures that are nominally parallel but highly overlapping in reality. On August 28, the officials specifically handled the State Central Military Commission positions. While the Party’s military positions still require separate public procedures , in terms of actual political reality, the original top military leadership team has indeed been shattered.

So today, let's discuss an interesting question: now that the Central Military Commission has been nearly emptied out, does Xi Jinping still dare to attack Taiwan? Many people, seeing the recent massive purge in the PLA, might first think: "That’s great, the generals are all being arrested, so what does the PLA have left to attack Taiwan with?" But is it really that simple? I personally feel there might be two completely opposite ways to interpret this. One is that Xi might now be even less likely to attack, but the other is even. more terrifying: once Xi has finished purging the military, he might actually be even more willing to strike. Which one is it? Actually, Xi Jinping's purging of the PLA didn't just start today. Soon after taking power in 2012, he began restructuring the military. You might be familiar with former CMC Vice Chairmen Xu Caihou and Guo Boxiong, or later, Fang Fenghui and Zhang Yang, though maybe you don't recognize them. Back then, many felt Xi was primarily clearing out military factions left over. from the Jiang Zemin era, while also tackling the severe issues of selling official positions and corruption within the PLA. That round of purges was already quite large in scale, but compared to the one launched in 2023, that earlier effort might just be considered an appetizer. Starting in 2023, first the Rocket Force had issues, then Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared and was dismissed; former Defense Minister Wei Fenghe was also handled. Next came Miao Hua, Director of the CMC Political Work. Department, and CMC Vice Chairman He Weidong. Then, by 2026, even Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were in trouble. The most shocking case here is Zhang Youxia, because he wasn't just any subordinate of Xi Jinping. He has long been viewed by the outside world as one of Xi's most important and loyal allies in the military, and he is also one of the few high-ranking PLA generals with actual combat experience— yet even Zhang Youxia is being investigated. So, this can no longer be simply explained as Xi removing old remnants to. replace them with his own people, because even those originally considered "his own" can now be arrested just the same. CSIS compiled a very worthy set of data in February 2026. They calculated that since 2022, at least 36 PLA generals and lieutenant generals have been formally purged or disciplined, while another 65 high-ranking officers have not appeared in public for a long time, presumably investigated or removed. In other words, if you count those who.

have disappeared, over 100 high-ranking PLA officers have been affected. Moreover, those taken down aren't concentrated in any single branch; they span the Army, Navy, Air Force, Rocket Force, Armed Police, and Theater Commands, as well as CMC departments responsible for joint operations, political work, and logistics and equipment. In fact, CSIS pointed out a very serious issue as early as February 2026: there were no longer any top-level leaders in the Central Military Commission with a background in operational systems; those. who remained were primarily from political work or disciplinary inspection backgrounds, rather than professional generals capable of managing large-scale joint operations. What we are seeing today is not just a few corrupt generals being arrested, but a drastic restructuring taking place within the entire PLA high command. Even by August 25th, the PLA publicly solicited leads on procurement violations within the Rocket Force, indicating that this round of purging is far from over. So the question is, if Xi Jinping is truly preparing to attack Taiwan...Why would he choose this exact moment to replace his highest-ranking generals one by one? If we look at this from a purely military perspective, I believe the answer is quite easy to understand. This , of course, affects the PLA's combat readiness, because attacking Taiwan is not like fighting a typical border war. Don't think for a moment that Xi can just sit in Beijing, say "Comrades, liberate Taiwan tomorrow at 8:00 AM," and hundreds of ships will just sail. over on their own. Launching a large-scale military operation against Taiwan—especially with the goal of an amphibious invasion and occupation— would likely be one of the most complex joint operations in modern military history. The PLA would first need to strike radar, airfields, and air defense systems; the Air Force must secure air superiority; the Navy must control the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters; the Army must prepare for amphibious landings; logistics must ferry troops, shells, fuel, and gear across the Strait ; all while managing electronic warfare. , cyber warfare, satellite intel, and drones—all must be synchronized, and if one link fails, the outcome could be entirely different. But now, the very people responsible for these tasks are getting into trouble one after another, the most typical example being Liu Zhenli. He was originally a chief of the Joint Staff Department. What is the Joint Staff Department? Simply put, it is the core unit within the PLA that is closest to knowing how a war would actually be fought. If you replace a business manager today , it might not necessarily affect the whole company.

But if you were preparing to launch the biggest project in history tomorrow, and the project director, technical lead, operations lead, and logistics lead were all under investigation, would you dare take on the job? A normal person would certainly hesitate . And even more seriously, this purge of generals doesn't just leave positions empty—it risks paralyzing the entire organization, making everyone afraid to make a decision. If you were a PLA general today, your predecessor was arrested, your predecessor’s predecessor was arrested,. your superior was arrested, your superior’s superior was arrested, and even Zhang Youxia, who everyone thought was close to Xi Jinping, was arrested— what would be your first goal when you go to work? Would it really be to study how to win a war in the Taiwan Strait? Or would it be to figure out how to avoid becoming the next Youxia? This is a very realistic question of human nature, and it is actually extremely dangerous for the military. Because one of the things most needed on the battlefield is for mid-to-lower-level commanders to make. judgments on their own under incomplete information. But in a highly politicized military where everyone looks out for themselves, the most common outcomes are "I don't want to make a mistake" and "I don't want to be held responsible"— people just follow orders and push everything up the chain of command. For a peacetime bureaucracy, this might just mean poor efficiency, but on the battlefield, it could be a matter of life and death. This brings up a second question: Why is Xi Jinping arresting so many people? Official CCP rhetoric always claims it's. anti-corruption, and this reason cannot be completely dismissed, because corruption in the PLA has historically been severe. You have to pay to get promoted, there's graft in construction, and arms procurement generates huge profits. So, Xi might truly believe that a corrupt military cannot win a war. From this perspective, his purge of the military has some military justification . But on the other hand, a purge on this scale creates another problem: If the Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission, the Defense Minister, the. Rocket Force commander, the Director of the Political Work Department, and the Chief of the Joint Staff all have issues one after another, doesn't that prove that Xi Jinping doesn't even trust his own military? If he truly believed the PLA was ready, why would he keep arresting people? Furthermore, the cost of a Taiwan Strait war is simply too high. If they lose, it wouldn't just be tens of thousands of troops lost; it would likely be the decades of military prestige the CCP has built up. They could face military intervention from the US, Japan, and.

other nations, and suffer international economic sanctions. China's exports, finance, technology, and energy supplies could all be severely impacted. More seriously, if Xi Jinping has framed the unification of Taiwan as his historical mission, but he ends up losing, it wouldn't just be a defeat for the PLA. It would be a personal failure, and could potentially turn into a political crisis for the CCP regime itself. So, following this logic, I believe these recent large-scale purges will indeed reduce the confidence to launch an. all-out war in the Taiwan Strait in the short term. This is not to say that the PLA lacks the capability to conduct blockades, military exercises, missile threats, or even localized military operations. In fact, even with the continuous purges of high-level officials, the PLA’s gray-zone pressure around Taiwan has never ceased. CSIS data also indicates that the CCP’s military and coast guard activities around Taiwan continue to increase this year, so we cannot simply say, "The PLA generals have all been arrested, so we. are now safe." That would be too optimistic. A more accurate statement would be that these purges increase the uncertainty of launching a large-scale joint operation , but they do not mean the CCP has lost the ability to use force. The expert survey conducted by CSIS this year is also quite interesting; only about 13%of the surveyed experts believe these purges are severe enough to prevent the CCP from using large-scale military force over the next two years, while about 57%believe the purges have. caused significant problems for military readiness, but not to the extent of rendering them unable to act. So, we cannot rejoice too soon, because the story does not end here. Now, let’s look at it from another angle : assume Xi Jinping purged the military not just because of corruption, but because he wanted to build an army that absolutely obeys the CCP Central Committee, and ultimately, absolutely obeys Xi Jinping’s orders. What would be the result? In the short term, it would certainly be chaotic because a large. number of high-level officials were replaced, but what if all the new generals are in place after a few years ? And all these new generals know that Zhang Youxia was purged, He Weidong was purged, Miao Hua was purged, Li Shangfu was purged, and Liu Zhenli was also purged. If even these top military officials, once considered Xi Jinping’s closest associates, could face trouble, what will those left behind learn? The answer is likely four words: absolute obedience. That is where the problem arises. If one day Xi Jinping truly decides to take action against.

Taiwan, no one would dare tell him, " Chairman, you can't; we aren't ready yet , the success rate of a landing isn't as high as you imagine, the U.S. might intervene, Japan might intervene, and we cannot bear the cost of economic sanctions." That is my real concern, because whether a nation’s military is dangerous depends not only on how many planes, warships, or fighters it has, but also on whether its top leader receives accurate information. People often ask if Xi Jinping will go crazy and attack Taiwan; I don't really. like that framing, because the person who starts a war doesn't necessarily think they are crazy. When many catastrophic wars are launched , the decision-makers may believe their judgment is perfectly rational; the real problem is what kind of information they are receiving. If everyone below knows exactly what the Chairman wants to hear, reports may gradually shift to saying the ROC military is demoralized, the U.S. won't dare intervene, our missiles can paralyze Taiwan, the conflict will end in days, and the Taiwanese people will welcome us. When one person says it,. then two, then ten, the world the supreme leader eventually sees may be completely different from reality; this is the classic risk of a highly centralized, autocratic system. Democratic systems are noisy— parliaments bicker, the media criticizes , and opposition parties attack—which allows for the open expression of dissenting views. It may look inefficient, but this noise serves a vital function: it can identify a mistake before the nation commits a grave one. However, a highly authoritarian system is the opposite. Decisions appear swift, with the. leader's word instantly executed by everyone below. The question is, what happens if the supreme leader is wrong? Who hits the brakes? Therefore, when observing the ongoing purges in the PLA, we shouldn't just ask how many generals are left; the real question is whether the remaining generals dare to tell Xi Jinping the truth. If the purge results in a more professional, better-connected, and more efficient military, it would certainly boost combat capabilities. But if it builds a military that values only loyalty over expertise—where they only report good news and never bad, claiming they will fulfill the Chairman’s tasks without anyone daring to say this war cannot be fought—that could actually be more dangerous for the Republic of China. Ultimately, with the Central Military Commission nearly hollowed out, does Xi Jinping still dare to attack Taiwan? My answer is that in the short term, it may be harder for him to fight, but that doesn't mean he is necessarily less likely to fight in the long term. The investigation of so many top-level officials will inevitably disrupt.

command, personnel, operational planning , and organizational trust. For a target like Taiwan, which requires extremely complex joint combat capabilities, long-term instability in the high command is certainly not a good thing. So, if someone claims Xi is preparing for an imminent full-scale invasion by dismantling his entire top military command team, I find that argument inherently contradictory. Conversely, we cannot assume the risk of a Taiwan Strait war has disappeared just because the Central Military Commission. is left with only two main members; Xi Jinping's goal may be to purge those he deems unreliable and rebuild a military command system he can control completely . If I were to condense today's conclusion into one sentence, it would be this: it might be harder for Xi Jinping to fight now, but that doesn't mean he wants to fight any less. What's even more concerning is that the biggest problem for the PLA today may not be a shortage of generals, but whether any of the remaining ones still dare to say no. A CCP that possesses. numerous missiles, nuclear weapons, aircraft carriers, and a complete industrial system is certainly cause for vigilance. However, a CCP that holds these weapons while centralizing all decision-making increasingly into the hands of one man, Xi Jinping, is perhaps even more alarming. This is because decisions of war and peace are no longer determined by collective discussion or the judgment of professional military commanders, but by what one man, Xi Jinping, truly believes. Therefore, the clearing out of the Central Military Commission—while some. might jokingly say it’s like gaining over 100 generals without firing a shot as in the days before the Civil War, or praising Comrade Xi for his "hard work" —is not entirely good news for the Republic of China. What we truly need to observe is whom Xi Jinping will appoint to fill these vacancies in the Central Military Commission next. Who will take control of the new Joint Staff Department, and will the high-level positions in the various military branches and theater commands be fully replenished? Will these people rise to power because of their professional competence, or because of their political loyalty? If the upper echelons of the PLA are gradually filled with those who are highly trusted by Xi Jinping, the question we will really need to ask is not whether the PLA can still fight, but when Xi Jinping truly gives the order to attack, who will be left to stop him? This may be the truly significant impact of this latest purge within the Central Military Commission on the situation in the Taiwan Strait. Having said this, I want to return to the purpose of this channel. What I have always wanted to discuss with everyone is that we care about the Taiwan Strait, the PLA, and.

whether Xi Jinping will start a war, primarily because we must defend the Republic of China and safeguard Taiwan's freedom and democracy. However, if we take a longer view of history, the real issue has never been just about Xi Jinping alone, nor about how many missiles or warships the Communist Party has today. It is about when the mainland can finally move beyond autocracy and establish a democratic republic with the people as its foundation. The National Revolution over 100 years ago sought to achieve more than just the. overthrow of the Qing government; it was not merely about replacing one group of rulers with another. It aimed to use the Three Principles of the People to build a modern nation that is nationally independent, where civil rights truly belong to the people, and where lives can be protected. This path later endured the era of warlords, the War of Resistance against Japan, and the Chinese Civil War, only to be interrupted by the totalitarian rule of the Communist Party.
